prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a class cannot be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) where individual damages questions will overwhelm common questions.

Cite at least six decisions of the Seventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The District Court Abused Its Discretion in Certifying a Rule 23(b)(3) Class Because Individualized Damages Questions Overwhelm Any Common Questions.

#### A. Rule 23(b)(3) demands a rigorous showing that common questions predominate.

Rule 23(b)(3) permits certification only if "questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members." Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3). A court must "make whatever factual and legal inquiries are necessary" to test that requirement, resolving disputes that bear on certification rather than presuming the plaintiff's allegations true. *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 675–76 (7th Cir. 2001); *Am. Honda Motor Co. v. Allen*, 600 F.3d 813, 815–16 (7th Cir. 2010) (court must resolve challenges to expert evidence on which certification depends). The inquiry turns on the evidence the parties will actually use. "If, to make a prima facie showing on a given question, the members of a proposed class will need to present evidence that varies from member to member, then it is an individual question." *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 815 (7th Cir. 2012). Plaintiffs bear the burden of proving predominance by a preponderance of the evidence. *Id.* at 811.

#### B. Plaintiffs' damages theory cannot be proven with common evidence.

Plaintiffs must show that damages are "capable of measurement on a classwide basis" and that their model "measure[s] only those damages attributable to" their theory of liability. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 34–35 (2013). They have not done so. Plaintiffs' proposed methodology [describe model] does not account for [variables, e.g., differences in product use, price paid, or mitigation], and the record shows that each class member's recovery would depend on [individual facts]. (*See* A__.) Calculating any member's damages would require evidence unique to that member, which is the kind of "evidence that varies from member to member" that *Messner* treats as an individual question. 669 F.3d at 815.

This Court has repeatedly reversed certification where individualized proof dominated. In *Andrews v. Chevy Chase Bank*, 545 F.3d 570, 573–76 (7th Cir. 2008), the Court reversed certification because the answers depended on the circumstances of each class member's own transaction. In *Sgouros v. TransUnion Corp.*, 817 F.3d 1029, 1034–35 (7th Cir. 2016), the Court reversed because individual inquiries into what each class member knew and understood could not be resolved with common proof. And in *Beaton v. SpeedyPC Software*, 907 F.3d 1018, 1029 (7th Cir. 2018), the Court vacated certification where the district court had not grappled with individualized questions about whether, and how, class members were affected. The same result follows here.

#### C. Individualized injury and damages inquiries cannot be separated from liability.

Plaintiffs will argue that individualized damages never defeat certification. That overstates the law. This Court has permitted a liability-only class with separate damages proceedings where damages could be handled mechanically or by homogeneous subgroups. *Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 800–01 (7th Cir. 2013). But *Butler* depended on common questions that were substantial and independent of the damages inquiry. Here, individual questions go to whether a class member was injured at all, not merely to the amount of the award. *See Oshana v. Coca-Cola Co.*, 472 F.3d 506, 513–14 (7th Cir. 2006) (affirming denial of certification where individualized questions of deception and injury would predominate). "[A] class should not be certified if it is apparent that it contains a great many persons who have suffered no injury at the hands of the defendant." *Kohen v. Pac. Inv. Mgmt. Co.*, 571 F.3d 672, 677 (7th Cir. 2009). The record shows that [a substantial portion] of the proposed class [was not harmed, or paid no premium, or benefited]. (*See* A__.) Sorting injured members from uninjured ones would require thousands of mini-trials, and Defendant would have a Seventh Amendment and due process right to contest each one.

Because these individualized determinations are unavoidable, the common questions Plaintiffs identify, such as [describe], would resolve only a small part of the litigation. Certification would not achieve the efficiencies Rule 23(b)(3) exists to secure.

#### D. Certification would improperly coerce settlement.

The cost of managing individualized proof also matters beyond efficiency. Certifying a class whose claims cannot be tried on common evidence places intense pressure on a defendant to settle regardless of the merits. *See In re Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc.*, 51 F.3d 1293, 1298–1300 (7th Cir. 1995) (cautioning against certification that induces settlement through the risk of an enormous judgment). That concern weighs heavily where, as here, the class device would not simplify the adjudication of individual damages.

The Court should reverse the order certifying the class.
